title: Bota Singh and Garja Singh
hookLine: tradition says two Sikhs set up a toll on the highway to prove the Khalsa was still alive

lines: A MAN HIDING BY THE ROAD.
cards: Two travelers pass a clump of bushes by the road. They glimpse a man hiding there, and one says to the other, loud enough to be heard: that can't be a Sikh. The Sikhs are finished.
And if any were left, they wouldn't hide. Tradition says the man in the bushes was Bota Singh, and that sentence stung him more than any sword.

teach.h: THE KHALSA IS FINISHED, THEY SAID.
teach.b: In the hunted years, tradition says, the governor's men claimed the Khalsa had been wiped out. Bota Singh had been living rough, slipping into Amritsar at night to bathe in the sacred pool and then disappearing again.
When he heard the travelers, he decided the claim needed an answer. So he and his companion Garja Singh walked out of hiding and did something almost absurd.

teach.h: A TOLL ON THE GREAT HIGHWAY.
teach.b: They picked a spot on the great highway near Tarn Taran, by a roadside inn, armed themselves with heavy clubs, and set up a toll. Every cart paid a small coin; every donkey, a smaller one.
And, tradition says, travelers paid. Nobody quite knew what to do with two Sikhs standing calmly in the middle of the road as if they owned it. Then Bota Singh did the boldest thing of all.
He wrote a letter to the governor in Lahore, telling him who was collecting tolls on the king's highway: a message that said, in effect, still here. Soldiers were sent. The two did not run.
Tradition says they fought until they fell. Notice what they were not doing. They were not stealing for themselves, and they were not trying to win a war two men could not win.
They were making a point only their presence could make: the Khalsa is alive. The travelers had said a Sikh would not hide. Bota Singh and Garja Singh decided that, this once, they would not.
Two clubs, a few coins, and a letter with a name on it.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Bota Singh and Garja Singh as a picture of chardi kala, high spirits under persecution, and it is often retold in gurdwara talks and children's classes.

games.q: you're Bota Singh, hiding by the road. you hear travelers say the Sikhs are finished, and that a real Sikh wouldn't hide. what do you do?
o: stay hidden; staying alive matters most.
step onto the highway and make the Khalsa's presence impossible to deny.
move to a safer place far away.

practice: Bring to mind one place where your presence would say something: a friend's hard day, a meeting you've been skipping, a family table you've been avoiding, a cause you've only watched.
Picture yourself walking in and simply being there, not giving a speech, not fixing everything, just present. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Bota Singh. The Sikh who, with Garja Singh, tradition says, set up a toll on the highway and wrote to the governor to prove the Khalsa was still alive.

carryVoice: Your line: still here. Sometimes simply being there is the whole message. Day eight hundred fifty, done.
